articles.headline: Treasury Designates Eight Canada-Based Entities for Facilitating Iranian Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced sanctions against eight Canada-based entities. These entities are accused of providing financial lifelines to the Iranian regime by enabling sanctioned Iranian entities to use their services, thereby facilitating the financing of terrorism and proxy groups.

Many of the designated entities are also involved in receiving and laundering funds associated with other criminal activities. This action was coordinated with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and FINTRAC, Canada's financial intelligence unit.

The designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian digital asset sector and other key sectors of the Iranian economy. This move follows previous OFAC sanctions on digital asset exchanges that have moved digital assets abroad on behalf of the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Sanctions on Cuba, Targeting Financial, Shipping, and Military Procurement Networks
body: The United States has announced fresh sanctions against eight entities and two individuals linked to Cuba's financial, shipping, and military procurement networks. The communist government in Havana is accused of sustaining activities considered a threat to American national security.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the sanctions target individuals and organizations connected to the Cuban regime's oil shipping operations, state-owned import and technical-support companies, and Chinese suppliers of military equipment. The State Department indicated that this action was carried out under Executive Order 14404, which authorizes sanctions against foreign individuals and organizations linked to repression in Cuba and activities threatening U.S. national security.

Among those targeted are Guillermo Faustino Rodriguez Lopez-Calleja, accused of involvement in offshore shipping companies moving Cuban crude oil, and Any Rodriguez Lastres, daughter of a previously sanctioned executive of the Cuban military-linked business conglomerate GAESA. Two Chinese companies, China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies, were also sanctioned for allegedly supplying military-related equipment and technology to Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ, Updates Iran Listings
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action also includes updates to certain Iran-related listings and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert.

These amendments follow earlier actions this year to ease restrictions on Venezuela's oil and gas sector, which began after the capture of Nicolás Maduro in January 2026. The U.S. government has expressed an intent to encourage private-sector participation and investment in Venezuela's energy sector.

The updated General License and FAQ aim to provide further clarity and guidance on permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program, which remains in force but has been eased through licenses.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment aims to provide updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

The issuance of amended general licenses is a routine measure by OFAC to adjust the scope of sanctions programs, often in response to evolving policy considerations or to clarify existing regulations.

While specific details of the amendment were not immediately released, such actions typically refine the parameters under which U.S. persons can engage in certain activities that would otherwise be prohibited by Iran sanctions.

articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Facilitators of DPRK IT Worker Schemes and DRC-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their roles in Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes. These schemes defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK's unlawful weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missile programs.

This action builds on OFAC's March 12, 2026, designation of a separate DPRK IT worker network, demonstrating Treasury's sustained commitment to dismantling illicit revenue-generating networks. The United States is joined by Australia and the European Union in designating individuals and entities supporting the DPRK's revenue generation and military activities.
In a separate action, OFAC also announced Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations, though specific details were not immediately available.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs Regarding Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates aim to provide clearer guidance to financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations.

The amendments likely address common questions and provide updated interpretations or procedures related to the reporting of blocked property and rejected transactions, which are critical components of sanctions compliance.
Such updates are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to ensure that regulated entities have the necessary information to effectively implement and adhere to U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related and Russia-Related General Licenses, Amends FAQs, and Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. These new licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

In addition to the new General Licenses, OFAC has also issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further clarity on various sanctions programs. The agency also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

The removal of designations for Belarus and North Korea indicates a recalibration of sanctions policy in specific instances, while the new General Licenses for Iran and Russia suggest targeted adjustments to facilitate certain activities or address humanitarian concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are aimed at combating intellectual property theft and protecting American innovation.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to mitigate any unintended consequences of the sanctions and to ensure that legitimate activities can continue.

The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to using sanctions as a tool to safeguard intellectual property rights and deter malicious actors who seek to exploit American technological advancements.

articles.headline: UK Updates Sanctions List with Correction for Russia Regime, Details Transport Sanctions
body: On November 3, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with a correction related to the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. The update included administrative amendments, with deleted information appearing in strikethrough and red, and newly added information underlined and highlighted in yellow.

The correction provided further details on transport sanctions, clarifying that a ship owned, controlled, chartered, or operated by a designated person is prohibited from entering a UK port, may be given movement or port entry directions, can be detained, and will be refused registration or have its existing registration terminated on the UK Ship Register. Similar prohibitions apply to aircraft.

The update also reiterated that making funds or economic resources available to a designated individual or entity subject to an asset freeze is prohibited for all persons who must comply with UK sanctions. The Secretary of State considers ZENITH GLOBAL CORPORATION LIMITED to be associated with Tahir GARAYEV, who is involved in supporting the Government of Russia through the energy sector.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List. This deregulatory action aligns export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of the newly controlled suppressors, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be available for suppressors.

Jeffrey I. Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, stated that this move is a 'common-sense' action that alleviates the compliance burden on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.
